title: How to make the AI produce less AI written content?
author: Ray_Light91
selftext:
So, when asking the AI come up with names or descriptions for items or speech bubbles content, the AI comes up with the most poetic content or randomly mashes words together.

Is there a way to guide the AI into producing better results?

Not item names like Depthveil Ore or whatever but actually something that feels diegetic and as if it has a history?

comments.author: bettertagsweretaken
comments.body:
You're going to have to come up with that level of detail on your own, aren't you? That's world-building, no? 

If you need names for weapons and places, then you need names for heroes and famous battles and other lived-in world experiences. The simplest solution is going to be to give it a name or a tactical space to occupy and ideate why someone would want that champion's item/castle/hilltop

replies.author: legojazzy
replies.body: Right, why would you even want to generate that particular type of content? Sure, use AI for code, game logic, even art. But for the things that make your game \*yours\*, you should really do it yourself. As much as AI is a poductivity boost, it just can't substitute taste and originality.

replies.author: ModernGameDev
replies.body:
I agree. The AI needs a bunch of context from the creator to really understand your world, its rules, and the characters. Things that have to come from the creator. AI can never excel in the imagination department. It needs something to work off from.

I believe a GDD really needs to make a comeback these days.

replies.author: Ray_Light91
replies.body:
I've actually made my own internal wiki that the AI uses and updates when relevant. Agents.md will read that for what the code is supposed to look like and how the came should function before it edits the codebase after a request. 

Still have to separate hardcoded player facing content like quests and text into an XML though.

replies.author: StandardStrange2038
replies.body: Writers block is real though. I've found just getting a generic list from AI in a certain topic can help spark me again when Im struggling to name something. Thats what name generators are for, people use them all the time.

replies.author: Ray_Light91
replies.body: This, Especially since English is not my native language. I can write and speak it at a decent level but I simply don't have the vocabulary that a native would. So it's nice to have AI generate a list of examples that help me rather than confuse me more.

replies.author: legojazzy
replies.body: I mean sure, I readily admit that I use alot of AI for brainstorming, it's just that it's a balancing act. Using too much AI = regression to the mean, and since everyone's using AI to brainstorm, we'll all end up with too much of the same content...

replies.author: StandardStrange2038
replies.body: That's not really an AI problem thats a content creation problem. There's only so much source material out there and the more we create the harder it becomes to create something actually unique and new.

replies.author: bettertagsweretaken
replies.body:
That's definitely the wrong way to look at it. 

You are the author. *We* are the authors. *We* get to determine the source material. Everything you create is unique and new. 

That doesn't mean it's good, though. You don't need to make something unique and new to be successful, you need to make a good game first.

replies.author: StandardStrange2038
replies.body:
Well yea... but thats the catch isn't it. Making a good game isn't some easy thing to do like you seem to be implying. You can make a "good game" that looks and feels just like everything else out there and no one will look twice at you because you've done nothing to stand out.

You also don't want to end up in the "Amazing concept, terrible execution" side of things either. But this isn't exclusively an AI problem which is the point I was making. AI helps you gather source material, but doesn't dictate what you do with it.

Maybe you should actually take a moment to understand what is being said before posting something ignorant.

comments.author: Cubey42
comments.body: "speech bubbles content" you mean like, dialog?

replies.author: Ray_Light91
replies.body: Yes, my bad! Will adjust. Thanks for the correction!

comments.author: kytheon
comments.body: You think an item called Depthveil Ore can't have a history or lore?

replies.author: Ray_Light91
replies.body: Sure it can! And if it fits, it fits! However, it feels like a compound word to me which makes it look more AI generated. Like 'FerriteIron Ingot' instead of 'Magnet' or Gloomshiver or Dawnshard.

comments.author: zenmatrix83
comments.body: How do I make my fish taste less like fish

comments.author: loopywolf
comments.body: If you ever figure out how to make AI be less verbose PLEASE SHARE IT!

replies.author: Ray_Light91
replies.body: I will! If AI can, then I will be able to, then there is hope for me yet!😂

replies.author: kytheon
replies.body: I tell it to. For example write it for 8 year olds, and it'll ease the complexity.

comments.author: Coreydoesart
comments.body: You can use AI to assist with it, but I’d just learn about etymology and the way humans have constructed names over the course of time. Look at how Tolkien developed his languages and names. Find sounds and names that you like. Don’t make the AI do that for you.

comments.author: Puzzleheaded_Act5292
comments.body: I’ve had better luck treating AI output like a messy first-pass writer rather than a lore generator. The biggest thing for me is giving it constraints that force specificity: who made the thing, what problem it solves, what people in-world complain about, what slang they use for it, etc. If the prompt is just “make fantasy ore names,” it’ll go straight to Depthveil/Ebonwhatever territory. But if you ask for something a tired miner, a greedy guild clerk, and a local superstition would all describe differently, the results usually feel way less generic.
